quotes  Piers  Plowman  : — 

"  And  therefore  he  shall  begge  and  bidde. 
And  no  man  bete  his  hunger."

1607,  we  gain  a  little  information  about  WhitecloaJc  : — "  There  remaineth  in  prison 
one  Thomas  Armestrong,  als  Whitecloake,  a  pestilent  fellowe,  who  is  accused  to  have 
gone  aboute  to  contrive  the  murdering  of  the  right  honorable  the  Lord  William 
Howard,  as  appeareth  by  examination  taken  before  some  Justices  of  the  Peace 
within  this  county.  Howsoever  for  the  harbouring  of  some  outlawes,  he  was  npon 
his  triall  acquitt  at  the  last  gaole  delivery  here  held,  yet  being  knoweu  heretofore 
to  have  practised  daungerously  the  hurt  of  the  country,  we  continew  him  still  in 
hold,  until  your  Lordship's  pleasures  be  further  knowen.  At  the  tyme  of  his  triall 
he  desired  banishment  into  Ireland,  yet  being  acquitt,  he  refuseth  the  same.  If 
your  Lordships  doe  not  think  it  fitt  he  be  urged  into  Ireland,  we  desire  he  and 
such  others  may  be  confined  to  the  cautionarye  towens,  or  sent  into  some  other 
service  in  the  warrs." — Dom  :  James  I.  xxvii.  13.

t  Juniper.  It  was  used  as  an  agreeable  addition  to  a  fire.  In  Bishop  Cosin's

X  Andirons,  i.  e.  moveable  irons,  placed  on  the  hearth  for  the  support  of  the 
wood  or  other  fuel.     The  word  occurs  in  Shakespeare  : — 

" Her  andirons 

were  two  winking  Cupids 

Of  silver,  each  on  one  foot  standing,  nicely 
Depending  on  their  brands." — Cymheline,  Act  ii.  So.  4. 

They  were  not  unfrequently  made  of  costly  material,  as  silver,  and  enriched  with 
curious  ornamentation.  Andirons  of  this  character  exist  at  Knowle,  and  in  brass 
or  iron  in  other  ancient  mansions. 

§  Small  iron  pans  with  feet,  for  cooking  purposes. 

jl  Pole-pieces,  straps  of  leather  attached  to  the  pole  of  the  coach,  and  connecting 
it  with  the  horses'  collars.

X  Andirons,  i.  e.  moveable  irons,  placed  on  the  hearth  for  the  support  of  the 
wood  or  other  fuel.     The  word  occurs  in  Shakespeare  : — 

" Her  andirons 

were  two  winking  Cupids 

Of  silver,  each  on  one  foot  standing,  nicely 
Depending  on  their  brands." — Cymheline,  Act  ii.  Sc.  4. 

They  were  not  unfrequently  made  of  costly  material,  as  silver,  and  enriched  with 
curious  ornamentation.  Andirons  of  this  character  exist  at  Knowle,  and  in  brass 
or  iron  in  other  ancient  mansions.

In  the  Strickland  Tower,  at  the  north-east  comer  of  the  existing  buildings,  ore 
found  the  remains  of  the  ancieut  keep.  This  tower  was  probably  built  by  Bishop

another  tower  was  built  by  Bishop  Bell,  on  the  north  front,  as  shown  by  his 
uianogram  on  the  cornice,  which  still  remains.  In  the  IGtb  century  further 
additions  were  made  by  Bishop  Kite,  who  built  the  tower  on  the  west  side,  which 
bears  his  monogram  and  sliield  of  arms,  impaling  those  of  the  Archbishopric  of 
Aimigh.  He  is  said  also  to  have  built  the  whole  of  that  side  of  the  quadrangle. 
Tlie  17th  century  witnessed  no  further  additions.  In  1645  it  was  ht-td  for  the 
lioyalists  by  Mr.  Lowther,  constable  of  the  castle,  but  was  taken  by  a  party  of 
Uol.  Heveringhani's  I'egimeut,  and  used  for  some  time  as  a  prison  for  the  Royalists. 
In  1648  it  was  again  garrisoned  by  a  company  of  the  Royalists,  and  alter  an 
asssnlt  of  two  hours  was  taken  by  storm,  and  burned  by  order  of  Col.  Cholmley.

£1161  11».  lOrf.  to  Col.  Heveringham.

the  parish  of  Haltwhistle)  belonged  to  the  Crown ;  but  in  1613  they  are  included 
in  a  Grant  to  llieophilus,  Lord  Howard  of  Wulden,  in  which  Plenmeller  and  all  iti 
stone  quarries  are  described  as  of  the  yearly  value  of  £3  6«.  Sd.,  and  Unthank,  then 
in  the  tenure  of  William  Ridley,  worth  20«.  a  year.  The  Inquest  after  Lord 
William's  death  describes  him  as  having  holden  of  the  Earl  of  Suffolk,  as  of  hit 
manor  of  Wark,  the  Lordship  of  Plenmeller,  and  the  messuages  and  lands  called

and  Byers  Park,  besides  several  other  places  in  the  parish  of  Haltwhistla. — Cf. 
Hodgson's  Hist.  Northumb.  II.  iii.  p.  343.

Howard  and  his  family.  In  1640  there  were  4  men  and  5  women  there,  as  we 
learn  from  the  account  of  wages  paid  in  that  year.  Askerton  Castle,  now  used  as  a 
farm-house,  is  a  very  interesting  specimen  of  a  small  Border  fortress.  The  type  of 
the  larger  castles  is  followed  upon  a  lesser  scale.  It  does  not  seem  to  have  grown 
put  of  a  pele  tower,  as  so  many  of  them  did,  but  to  have  been  built  in  its  present 
form  at  one  time,  or  nearly  so.  Two  square  towers  flank  the  central  part  of  the 
building,  which  faces  the  south.  There  is  a  peculiarity  in  the  arrangement  of  these 
towers  which  may  be  most  intelligibly  explained  by  the  diagram  here  g^ven. 

The  angles  formed  respectively 

^?^ at  a  and  b  have  been  contrived 

to  accommodate  the  external 
apertures  of  the  latrines  in  the 
upper  stories  of  each  tower.  The 
initials  T.  D.  on  the  weather- 

moulding  of  the  south-western 

g  tower  seem  to  identify  Thomas, 

Lord  Dacre,  as  the  builder. 
Behind  is  a  small  quadrangle  with  a  curtain  wall  to  the  east  and  the  stabling  to 
the  north.  Over  the  latter  have  been  apartments,  as  is  shown  by  old  fireplaces 
and  mullioned  windows,  now  walled  up,  but  all  in  their  original  position.  The 
space  is  now  used  as  a  hay-loft.  The  western  side  of  the  little  quadrangle  is 
occupied  by  a  building  attached  to  the  south-western  tower,  which  was  probably 
the  hall.  It  has  a  3-light  window  at  its  northern  end,  probably  inserted  by  Lord 
William  Howard.  Each  tower  has  very  small  square  openings  to  the  south  for  the 
admission  of  light  and  air,  high  up  in  the  wall.  Similar  openings  occur  in  the 
upper  story  of  the  central  building.  The  other  windows  in  this  portion  are 
modern,  except  a  2.1ight  mullioned  one  of  16th  century  work.  In  the  apartment 
now  occupied  as  a  kitchen  is  a  wide  arched  fireplace,  on  the  mantle  of  which  is 
carved  in  low  relief  Thomas  CAELEToy.  Iitniob.  1576.  In  a  communi- 
cation addressed  to  Lord  Burleigh  in  1592  by  Edward  Aglionby,  concerning  the 
means  of  defence  on  the  Borders,  Thomas  Carleton,  Esq.  is  mentioned  as  being 
**  Land-serjant  of  Gilsland,**  who,  it  is  stated,  "  ought  to  lye  at  Askerton  Castle." 
— Bibl.  Reg.  xviii.  D.  iii.  fol.  70.  (Published  in  the  Archseologia  for  1827.)

•f*  Bisk,  bisque y  a  term  in  cookery  for  a  rich  kind  of  pottage,  made  of  quails,  capons,

&amp;c.;  rennet,  usually  the  stomach  of  a  calf  properly  prepared.  A.  S.  ceaelib,  cyslib,

Cleveland  loppered,  coagulated  or  curdled.— Cf.  Atkinson's  Cleveland  Glossary,  s.v.

Household  Books.    Sir  John  was  son  of  Sir  Edward  Wintonr,  by  Anne,  danghter 
of  Edward,  Earl  of  Worcester.    He  was  a  zealous  Catholic,  and  a  most  de?oted 
royalist.    His  house  at  Lydney  was  fortified  and  garrisoned  by  him  during  tbe 
civil  wars,  and  defended  against  repeated  attacks  made  upon  it  by  detachments 
from  the  parliamentary  forces  stationed  at  Gloucester.    He  had  been  secretary  to 
the  Queen,  and  few  men  were  regarded  with  more  avernon  by  those  who  wen 
ranged  on  the  side  of  the  Parliament.    Before  the  troubles  he  had  received  in 
extensive  grant  from  the  Crown  of  woods,  waste  land,  quarries,  and  mines,  in  the 
Forest  of  Dean,  and  was  evidently  carrying  on  iron  worss  and  collieries  with  tlie 
energy  which  was  a  prominent  feature  in  his  character.    Boring  for  coal  must  hare 
been  an  unknown  thing  in  the  Forest  of  Dean,  for  we  find  that  some  person  skilled 
in  that  operation  was  not  long  afterwards  sent  to  Lydney  by  Lord  Wilfiim 
Howard.    The  manor  of  Lydney  was  granted  by  Queen  Elizabe^  to  Sir  William 
Wintour,  the  grandfather  of  Sir  John,  for  his  gallant  services  as  Vice-Adminl 
against  the  Spanish  Armada.    He  built  Lydney  House  (then  caXied  White  Cron) 
about  1588.     It  was  burnt  by  Sir  John  Wintour  to  prevent  its  being  occupied  bjr 
the  parliamentarian  forces,  and  the  remains  were  after  the  war  converted  mto  an 
iron  furnace. — Cf.  Atkyns'  Gloucestershire,  p.  539;  Bibliotheca  Gloucestrensie,  L 
Ixxxii.  Ixxxvii. ;   Commons'  Journals,  Feb.  15,  1641-2;  Thurloe's  State  Fapen» 
I.  80.    During  the  Protectorate  Sir  John  Wintour,  like  many  of  the  Boyalists^  seems 
to  have  lived  by  his  wits.     In  1656  he  had  a  project  for  *'  charring  sea-coale,*'  or, 
in  modern  language,  turning  it  into  coke.    But  his  scheme  met  with  no  enoonrage* 
ment.     See  Evelyn's  Diary  (July  11,  1656). 

*  Anne,  Countess  Dowager  of  Arundel,  daughter  and  co-heir  of  Lord  DaVB» 
•and  widow  of  Philip,  the  unfortunate  Earl  of  Arundel,  who  died  in  the  ToW 
Oct.  19, 1595,  whilst  under  condemnation  for  high  treason.  By  him  the  had  two 
children,  JBlizabeth,  who  died  in  her  sixteenth  year,  and  Thomas,  who  was  aftff- 
wards  restored  to  the  forfeited  honours  of  the  Earldom.  Lady  Amndel  rarnred 
him  thirty-five  years,  dying  at  Shefnal  Manor  in  Shropshire,  April  18,  IM 
in  the  seventy-fourth  year  of  her  age.  She  was  buried  in  the  same  vault  with 
her  husband  in  the  collegiate  chapel  at  Arundel.  She  had  experienced  all  the 
rancour  of  Queen  Elizabeth's  hatred,  and  was  constantly  exposed  to  insult  and 
persecution.  As  soon  as  the  Earl's  condemnation  was  pronounced,  his  eatatn 
were  confiscated  to  the  crown,  his  houses,  furniture,  and  other  property  were 
seized  for  the  benefit  of  the  Queen,  and  "  nothing,"  says  her  biographer,  **  was  left 
her  but  the  beds  whereon  herself,  children,  and  some  few  servants,  were  to  take 
their  rest,  and  those  only  lent  her  for  a  time."  The  very  pension  that  was  doled 
out  to  her  for  her  subsistence  was  never  paid  with  punctuality,  and  seldom  with- 
out entreaties ;  whilst,  for  her  own  inheritance,  which  on  the  death  of  her  husband 
should  instantly  have  reverted  to  her,  she  was  compelled,  after  a  moltipUcity  of 
vexatious  delays,  to  compound,  by  the  sacrifice  of  nearly  10^000^. — Cf.  lRenef% 
Hist.  Arundel,  pp.  411 — £l3.

*  Aug.  30,  1640.  On  the  27th  August  the  king  received  intelligence  from  Lord 
Conway  that  the  Scotch  had  invaded  England,  and  would  that  night  be  near 
Newcastle  with  their  army.  On  that  day  the  Scotch  encamped  near  Newbum. 
The  engngement  took  place  the  next  day,  when  the  king's  forces  were  defeated. 
On  the  29th  Lord  Conway  and  Sir  Jacob  Astley  drew  off  their  troops  to  Durham, 
leaving  Newcastle  defenceless.  In  the  afternoon  of  that  day  Sir  Peter 
Kiddell,  on  threat  of  bombardment,  opened  the  gates  of  Newcastle  to  the  Scotch. 
On  Monday,  the  31st,  Lesley  came  and  pitched  his  tents  on  Gateshead  Hill,  half  a 
mile  south  of  Newcastle.  Sept.  3.  Great  alarm  felt  by  the  inhabitants  of  New- 
castle, who  fled  in  great  numbers.  Same  at  Durham. — Rushworth,  Part  II.  vol  iL 
p.  1234,  ct  seqq.

appeal,  was  confirmed  by  the  committee  for  plundered  ministers.  Morland  was

teen Judges  concurred  in  it. 

t  Robert,  sixth  Lord  Crichton  of  Sanquhar.  He  lost  an  eye  in  a  trial  of  skill  with 
a  fencing-master  named  John  Turner,  against  whom  in  consequence  he  conceived  a 
violent  hatred,  and  in  May,  1612,  he  hired  two  Scotchmen,  Chny  and  Cariisle^  to

June  before  the  gates  of  Westminster  Hall.

The  next  morning  we  happily  lighted  on  a  guide,  who  by  chance 
was  bound  for  those  intricate  wayes,  a  perfect  intelligencer  was  he, 
and  we  did  imagine  him  to  be  some  processe  carryer,  or  some  mes- 
senger, or  informer,  that  used  to  visit  those  northeme  parts,  for  he 
was  both  perfect  in  the  wayes,  and  the  places  of  the  cheife  men,  in 
those  countryes.  With  him  we  mounted  for  Carlile,  still  along  by 
the  Piets'  wall,  the  wayes  we  found  as  mountainous,  rocky,  and  dan- 
gerous as  those  the  daye  before,  but  not  so  tedious,  in  respect  we  had 
a  good  guide.  Many  ancient  castles  and  seats,  and  some  parkes,  we 
pass'd  by  in  our  sight  on  both  hands,  bat  more  especially  (as  we  are 
specially  bound  to  that  house)  wee  did  not  let  passe,  the  stately  and 
fayre  Castle  of  Naworth,  with  that  large,  ston'd  walled  parke,  wherein 
many  lieards  of  deere  doe  feed  on  such  high  mountaines  as  com- 
maunds  and  overtops  the  whole  country  thereabouts,  and  some  part 
of  the  neit  adiacent  kingdomo.  The  parkes,  liberties,  and  forrest, 
that  doth  belong  to  that  noble  old  lord,  all  togeather,  within  the 
compassH  of  his  own  territories,  I  dare  (hearing  the  same  verefy'd 
from  his  Lordship's  owne  mouth)  averre  to  be  as  great  a  (juantity 
logeather  in  one  place,  as  any  one  other  Lord  bath  whatsoever.

forget  to  tell  you  what  lucky  entertainment  wee  met  with  in  a  little 
poore  cottage  in  his  liberties,  driven  in  thibher  with  very  ill  weather, 
to  wit,  a  cup  of  nappy  ale,  and  a  peece  of  a  red  deere  pye,  more  then 
we  thought  fit  to  acquaint  his  Lordship  with. 

Not  long  before  we  came  into  his  Lordship's  large  territoriie  of 
Gilsland,  we  pass'd  the  Picts'  wall,  which  runs  quite  through  tiie 
counties  of  Northumberland  and  Cumberland,  begining  at  Walsend, 
neere  the  east  sea,  upon  the  river  of  Tyne,  and  ending  at  the  weat 
sea,  a  little  beyond  Carlile,  which  the  Eomane  Emperors  finrt  mads 
8  foot  broad,  and  12  foot  high,  and  80  mile  long,  and  there,  OTeri 
little  rivolet,  we  entred  into  the  next  county,  the  place  where  tiie 
High  Sherifie  receives  the  Judges  with  many  attendfuit  bonnetts  and 
gallowayes,  and  heere  we  left  Tyne  to  seeke  his  head,  not  hi  from 
Tees.  From  that  place  to  Warwicke  Bridge  we  pass'd  all  the  way 
over  that  Lord's  liberties  and  franchises,  and  then  over  the  river 
Eden,  by  a  fayre  arch't  bndge,  and  to  end  our  second  weeke'g  travel], 
passing  the  little  brooke  Petterell,  we  came  safe  and  well,  though  well 
wet,  to  our  inne,  the  Angell,  in  the  market  place  in  that  old  etrong 
citty  of  Carlile,  built  by  a  British  king  neere  1000  yeeres  before 
Christ ;  for  of  these  two  properties,  antiquitie  and  strength,  it  may 
cheifely  boast,  it  being  otherwise,  both  for  revenues,  buildings,  and 
the  inhabitants  and  their  condition,  very  poore. 

The  next  day  we  repayr'd  to  their  Cathedrall,  which  is  nothing  soe 
fayre  and  stately  as  those  we  had  seene,  but  more  like  a  great,  wild 
country  church ;  and  as  it  appear'd  outwardly  so  was  it  inwardly, 
neither  beautify'd  nor  adom'd  one  whit.  1  remember  no  more  monur 
ments  of  note  but  that  of  Bishop  Oglethorpe,  that  crowned  oar  late 
vertuous  Queene  Elizabeth ;  and  that  of  Snowden,  the  Bishop  that 
preach'd  Eobin  Hood  to  our  late  renowned  king.  The  organs  and 
voices  did  well  agree,  the  one  being  like  a  shrill  bagpipe,  the  other 
like  the  Scottish  tone.  The  Sermon,  in  the  like  accent,  was  such  as 
wee  would  hardly  bring  away,  though  it  was  deliver'd  by  a  neat 
young  schoUer,  (sent  that  morning  from  Rose  Castle,  the  Bish(^*8 
Mansion,  which  stands  upon  Rose  and  Cawd  rivers)  one  of  the 
Bishop's  chaplaines,  to  supply  his  Lord's  place  that  day.  The  Com- 
munion also  was  administred,  and  receiv  d  in  a  wild  and  unieverent 
manner. 

To  leave  the  Church  we  made  bold  a  little  with  the  day  to  view 
the  citty,  and  in  it  the  cheife  place,  the  strong  and  fayre  Castle,  built 
by  William  Rufus  upon  a  rocke,  close  by  the  river,  which  cornea  from 
Appleby,  on  the  north  side  of  the  citty  towards  Scotland,  over  wfaieh 
river  there  is  a  fayre  stone  bridge  of  9  or  10  arches,  about  8  milei 
from  the  sea.  When  we  were  on  the  top  of  the  Castle,  we  eaiOy 
discem'd  the  silver  sands  that  in  that  place  part  the  two  kingdomei, 
and  neere  to  them  Burgh  on  the  Sands,  where  King  Edward  the  flrrt 
breathed  his  last ;  Great  Nay  Church  and  Brunswicke  hill  in  Seot- 


land  we  at  the  same  time  did  see,  which  sight  did  sufficiently  aatiBiy 
us,  without  the  curiosity  or  paines  of  travelling  thither. 

This  ancient  citty  hath  i'elt  much  of  the  feirceness  of  the  hordering 
Scotts,  which  hath  caus'd  her  to  be  guarded  with  hb  strong  and  defen- 
sible a  wait  and  cittadella  as  any  other  in  England,  through  which 
wee  enter  her  by  three  strong  gates.  It  makes  shift  to  maintaine  a 
Mayor,  distinguish'd  by  his  white  staffe,  and  12  Aldermen  liis 
brethren,  sans  cap  of  maintenance,  hut  theii-  blew  bonnets,  which  they 
are  as  proud  in  as  our  southeine  cittizens  in  their  heavers.  Two  of 
the  Aldermen,  being  very  worthy  knights,  doth  grace  and  coun- 
tenance their  company,  and  poore  citty,  not  a  little,  soe  the  grave 
Recorder  dotb,  being  a  knight  also,  [Jjt  marg :  S'.  Eichard  Graham 
and  S'.  George  Dalston.     S'.  Tho.  Carleton,  itecorder.] 

Whilst  we  were  thus  rounding,  facing,  counter-marching,  and 
wheeling,  in  this  strong  garrison  towne,  wo  heard  of  a  mesBenger 
from  that  truly  noble  Lord  we  the  last  day  miss'd  on  at  Naworth, 
with  a  curteous  invitation  to  dinner  at  Corby  Castle  the  next  day, 
(for  there  his  Lordship  then  was)  which  we  accompted  (as  it  was 
indeed)  a  mighty  favour  from  soe  noble  a  person,  and  sent  backe 
his  Lordship's  servant  with  the  tender  of  our  services  till  the  next 
day,  that  we  were  to  wayte  upon  his  Lordship  to  present  them  our 
selves. 

The  next  day  wee  went  thither,  and  were  by  that  generous  bravo 
Lord  curteously  and  nobly  ontertayn'd,  and  sorry,  be  aayd,  he  was, 
that  hee  was  not  at  Naworth  to  give  us  then  the  !il;e.  His  Lord- 
ship's commaunds  made  us  to  transgresse  good  manners,  for  neither 
would  he  suffer  «s  to  speake  uncover'd,  nor  to  stand  up  (although 
our  duty  requir'd  another  posture)  but  plac'd  us  by  his  Lordship  him- 
selfe  to  discourse  with  him  until!  dinner  time. 

Anon  appear'd  a  grave  and  vertuous  matron,  his  Honorable  Lady, 
who  told  us,  indeed  we  were  heartily  welcome,  and  whilst  our  Ancient 
and  my  selfe  addreas'd  our  selves  to  satisfy  his  Lordship  in  such 
occurrences  of  Norfolke  as  be  pleas'd  to  aske,  and  desir'd  to  know, 
wee  left  our  modest  Captaine  to  relate  to  his  noble  Lady  what  she 
desir'd.  These  noble  twaine  (as  it  pleas'd  themselves  to  tell  us 
themselves)  could  nott  make  above  25  yeeres  both  tt^eather,  when 
first  they  were  marry'd,  that  now  can  make  above  140  yeares,  and 
are  very  hearty,  well,  and  merry,  and  long  may  they  continue  soe, 
for  soe  have  they  all  iust  cause  to  pray,  that  live  neere  them,  for 
their  hospitality  and  fre  entertainment,  agrees  with  their  generous 
and  noble  extraction,  and  their  yeeres  retaines  the  memory  of  their 
honorable  predecessors'  bountifull  house  keeping.

ADDENDA. 


Mb,  Nicholas  EoacAEBOCK.* 

The  name  of  Mr.  Boscarrock  occurs  very  frequently  in  the  House- 
bold  Books  of  Naworth  Castle,  which  seema  to  havi;  been  his  home 
irom  the  year  1607,  if  not  before,  until  hia  death.  (See  ante,  pp.  6, 
7,  n.)  Nicholas  Koscarrock  was  the  fifth  son  of  Richard  Boscarrock, 
Esquire,  of  Eoacarrook,  by  Isabella,  daughter  of  Riebard  Trevenor, 
and  heir  of  her  brother,  William  Trevenor.  His  father,  during  his  life- 
time, settled  upon  him  the  estates  of  Fenhale,  Carbura,  and  Newton, 
in  the  parishes  of  St.  Cleer  and  St.  German's,  in  Cornwall,  (See  Sir  J, 
Maclean's  History  of  Trigg  Minor,  \.  558.)  "  His  industrious  delight 
in  matters  of  history  and  antiquity,"  which  Carew  makes  mention  of, 
is  corroborated  from  other  sources  of  information.  In  1572  there  was 
published  by  Richard  Tottell,  "the  Workeg  of  Armor ie,  deuyded  into

The  site,  which  is  on  slightly  rising  ground,  abont  a  quarter  of  a

fortresB The  fosse  is  of  a  rectangular  figure,  eiaetly  following

ravelin  lying  within  the  moat,  and  provided  with  a  ditcb  of  its  own. 
It  is  nearly  square,  the  dimensions  are  45  feet  by  40  feet ;  it  is  on  the 
same  level  as  the  inner  enclosure,  and  the  sides  presented  to  the 
exterior  are  nearly  flush  with  the  lines  of  scarp  of  the  main  ditch. 
The  function  of  this  earthwork  Jias  been  to  flank  the  main  entrance 
and  drawbridge,  which  probably  were  placed  where  the  gap  aow  is, 
about  the  middle  of  the  western  side.  There  remain  no  traces  of 
buildings  of  gatehouse,  or  of  gatehouse  towers,  or  of  barbican,  and 
there  may  have  been  none,  except  the  timber  apparatus  for  the  draw- 
bridge— there  has  been  no  masonry  along  the  edge  of  the  moat,  the 
defence  has  been  by  wooden  stockading. 

The  piSh  of  the  castle  seems  to  have  been  quadrangular,  forming  a 
square  of  about  150  feet,  yet  not  regular  nor  complete,  seeing  that  the 
eastern  line  re-enters  at  an  angle,  at  the  southern  comer,  leaving  thire 
a  rectangular  recess. 

■  Two  towers,  of  which  a  good  deal  still  remains,  though  plundered  of 
their  faeing-stones,  cap  the  angles  on  the  south  face.  They  are 
nearly  of  the  same  size  and  pattern  and  nearly  square,  35  by  30  feet ; 
they  are  about  50  lect  apart,  and  set  on  nearly  flush  with  the  curtain 
wall  which  has  connected  them.  They  have  had  a  basement,  and  a 
first  and  second  floor.  The  basement  in  each  consists  of  a  vaulted 
chamber,  entered  from  the  ward,  at  the  court  level,  by  a  narrow  door- 
way with  a  pointed  arch,  aud  plainly  chamfered ;  each  is  lighted  with

a  single  square-headed  loop.  In  the  interior  these  chambers  are  irdt

On  turning   to   the   north    side  of  the  enceinte  there   standi  i

The  tower  has  been  constructed  solely  with  the  object  of  canying 
the  winding  staircase,  which  has  given  access  to  three  stories  of  upper

outer  buildings.  This  side  of  the  quadrangle  has  contained  the  noge

chapel.

This  ball,  if  we  rely  on  history  and  tradition,  cannot  have  been

We  may  consider  the  hall,  and  the  buildings  connected  with  it,  and

Sandford,  who  visited  this  place  about  1610,  says  in  his  MSS., 
"  this  great  castle  of  Kirkoswald  was  oncu  the  fairest  fabric  that  ever

hall,  and  of  all  his  succeeding  successors  Kings  of  England  portraicted 
to  the  waist,  their  visage,  hats,  feathers,  garbs,  and  habits,  in  the  roof 
of  this  hall ;  now  translated  to  Naward  Castle,  where  they  are  placed 
!□  the  roof  of  the  hall,  and  at  the  end  thereof.  This  castle  was  the 
ancient  palace  of  the  Loi-d  Multon,  mai-rying  the  Jjord  Vaui's  heir, 
lord  of  Naworth  and  Gilsland ;  and  afterwards  of  the  late  Lords 
Dacre  ;  and  now  come  by  lineal  deseent  to  the  tresgallant  the  Earla 
of  Sussex  i  with  the  lands  adjoining,  and  many  brave  parka  and  vill^ea 
belonging  thereto."

Let  us  now  turn  to  the  western  face,  or  front  of  the  atceinte. 
Amid  the  hillocks,  and  hollows,  and  heaps  of  grass-grown  rubbish, 
that  encumber  this  side  of  the  ruin,  it  is  possible  to  indicate  the  site 
of  the  gateway  as  having  consisted  of  an  outer  and  inner  gate, 
flanked  with  turrets,  or  tower-like  buttresses.  It  was  usual  in  the 
outer  biiilej,  outside  of  the  walls,  to  have  the  stabling,  out-offices, 
and  inferior  apartments — the  site  of  these  may  be  traced  in  the 
foundation  of  main  walls  and  partitions,  covered  by  the  turf,  ex- 
tending from  the  northern  boundary  of  the  castle  to  the  scarp  of  the 

It  ia  possible  that  the  road  of  approach  to  the  castle  gate,  from 
the  drawbridge  and  the  moat,  was  sunken  below  the  level  of  the 
ground,  in  the  manner  of  a  trench  or  covered  way,  so  as  to  shelter 
the  advance  or  retreat  of  the  defenders  ;  the  depression  in  the  ground 
suggests  the  idea. 

To  sum  up  what  can  be  told  of  the  antiquity  of  Kirkoswald  Castle. 
I  would  say — there  is  no  part  of  it  to  which  an  earlier  date  can  be 
assigned  than  the  beginning  of  the  fourteenth  century.  The  inceptive 
work  of  Ilandolph  Engain  has  been  of  no  account, — the  Norman  has 
left  no  mark  here — there  is  no  smgle  massive  keep  nor  citadel, — 
the  invariable  characteristic  of  the  strong  Norman  fortress,  and 
which  we  find  abiding  almost  m  its  piistine  strength,  when  the 
adjacent  buildings  of  a  subsequent  date  are  mouldering  in  ruins. 

The  two  original  toners  afford  the  key  to  its  design  and  pro- 
portions, as  a  small  Edwardian  Caatle,  that  is,  a  quadrangular  mural 
enclosure,  with  projecting  towers  capping  the  angles.
